CONTENT WARNING
Within the presentation of Arkham’s locations, people, and history are various aspects that some Keepers and players may find
distressing, most notably suicide, violence against children, abortion, animal cruelty, and discrimination and racism regarding
some NPC attitudes, historical mention of the slave trade, and a lack of diversity within some Arkham institutions. Equally, the
witches depicted are, mostly, drawn from the well of horror fiction and do not represent modern-day adherents. While such
content is predominantly “off screen,” the Keeper should consider and discuss such matters with their group before play begins,
enabling the Keeper to adjust their presentation of Arkham to maintain everyone’s comfort levels, including their own. Arkham
is historically a predominantly white and conservative town—your Arkham doesn’t have to be, so change it to suit your vision.
Adjusting aspects problematical for your play group is easy to do, whether by toning such aspects down, removing any overt
depiction, or by changing them entirely. Presentation is key, especially in a horror game, and understanding where to cut or to
draw a veil and fade to black is a useful skill for the Keeper to employ so that it doesn’t diminish anyone’s enjoyment of the game.

Crime
Outside of the mobsters, murders, kidnappings, burglaries, fisticuffs,
and drunken and indecent behavior are viewed by the Arkham
establishment and its wealthy elite as the behavior of the poor, the
uneducated, and immigrants. Of course, in reality, such crimes can
be committed by anyone; it’s just that those in power tend to have
the means or connections to get away scot-free. Thus, the occasional
burglary of a fine home or an important shop reaps headlines, while
the disappearance of a poor child doesn’t raise an eyebrow.
In terms of a hierarchy of crime, if low-rent burglars and muggers
are at the bottom and mobsters at the top, then Arkham street
gangs fill the middle of the pyramid. Made up of teenagers (mostly
boys) who have little future and lots of time, such street gangs are
“family” for most. Being a member grants a level of security and
prestige, as well as a acting a potential pathway to getting noticed
by the “big boys” like Danny O’Bannion (Lucky Clover Cartage
Co., 412) or Joe Potrello (The Italian Club, 912). Arkham’s two
most notable street gangs are the Rocks (Southside Gym, 717) and
the Finns (Dunham’s Brickyard, 517), respectively ethnic Italian
and Irish. They incidentally lie, cheat, and steal, but mostly they
gather to swear, boast, and gain respect. They know their place in
the pecking order, never causing trouble in wealthy neighborhoods
as they know the police will be unmerciful. These gangs have their
hangouts, where the members meet in the afternoons, sauntering
and swaggering as they go nowhere. Historically, large fights have
broken out between the two gangs, but, in recent times, these have
become less frequent. Presently, gangs are observing territorial
boundaries—but that can easily change in the blink of an eye.
Organized Mobs
Some of Arkham’s placid character has changed since the
Eighteenth Amendment, which barred the sale and use of alcohol
for consumption on January 16, 1920. Like many places, Arkham
never really went “dry.” Imbibers, anticipating lean years, hoarded
beer, wine, and liquor. As those sources began to be exhausted, illegal
liquor distribution networks from Canada and Europe grew and
evolved. The money followed, as did turf wars and price competition.
Back to the days of the rum trade, alcoholism in the US was
epidemic, linked with innumerable cruelties and brutalities,
but the systematic prohibition against alcoholic beverages
establishes systematic crime, concentrating fortunes in the
hands of ambitious criminals.

TABLE: ARKHAM REPUTATIONS
Record an investigator’s current status in the My Story or Personal Description boxes on their Investigator Sheet.
Status Descriptor Social Interaction
Well respected; noted for good works in the community; authority
Celebrated Two bonus dice
figure; somewhat famous.
Distinguished Seen as doing good; honorable mention in newspaper; local hero. One bonus die
Respectable Average person; undistinguished. No bonus or penalty dice
Seen acting suspiciously or oddly; in trouble with police; accused/
Shameful One penalty die
convicted of crime; bad press; considered a scoundrel.
Known criminal; disreputable; dishonorable; lots of bad press;
Notorious Two penalty dice
untrustworthy; considered malicious or plain bad.
Applying the Modifiers
When applying a modifier to a social interaction the Keeper should consider the status of the NPC concerned—whether they are
“villainous” or “heroic”—as the modifier could change from a bonus to a penalty, and vice versa. Usually, the modifier remains the
same, but the Keeper should consider reversing it when they feel the situation warrants it, as determined by whom the NPC is and
their view of the investigator. For example, a Shameful investigator normally gets a penalty die, but if they were trying to Persuade
a local crime boss, the penalty may become a bonus as the investigator is known for being shady, so gains merit with the criminal.

11 awful porcupines, with long fingers and faces that stood on two legs, who liked nothing more than to trick and kill folk traveling through their land,

12 into the water to drown. My grandpa said ole Jenny came from a place called Shropshire in England, and was brought over by the English when they
first came here.

13
all bloodied, and burned him alive to rid themselves of the evil. Fearing that Jack would come back, they wrapped his bones in iron and buried him

chapter 4
The front of the building (W Main Street) contains offices,
with the rear being the warehousing space; the warehouse doors
open onto W River Street, providing easy access to the riverside
docks and road. A small maintenance workshop sits next door,
with room to park various trucks.
A Smart Operation
While Lucky Clover provides legitimate business services, it is
also a front for the bootlegging operations in Arkham, and run by
Danny O’Bannion, who grabbed the business from Joe Potrello
(The Italian Club, 912). Bootlegged liquor is loaded from boats at
the river docks (410) and stored here before being transported to
quench Arkham’s thirst.
Since his takeover, O’Bannion’s sales have boomed. Originally, Joe
Potrello had trucked in booze from Boston, but this has proved to
be insufficient and so a new approach was called for, with whiskey,
gin, and other liquor loaded onto small motor launches from a ship
anchored off Kingsport, beyond the 12-mile (19 km) limit. In the
dead of night, the motorboats return to the Miskatonic estuary
north of Kingsport and, in the dark, running lights off, make their
way upriver to Arkham.
Once outside town, the boats kill their motors and wait at anchor
for the next scheduled freight train to pass through Arkham. When a
train approaches Arkham, the boats head upriver, the passing freight
muffling their noise. If timed right, the boats reach the wharves while
the noisy freight rumbles through. The craft tie up, and a waiting
crew quickly unloads it, stashing the booze into the Lucky Clover
Cartage Co. warehouses.
From here, the operation disperses the booze to volume retailers, such
as The Speakeasy (113), Sycamores (920), and the Arkham General
Store (504), which, in turn, may supply smaller dealers. Helped by
payoffs to police officers, the routine works admirably, such that Arkham
has become a key distribution point for nearby communities, including
Aylesbury, Rowley, Ipswich, Newburyport, and Innsmouth.
O’Bannion’s Crew
While O’Bannion’s crew is majority Irish, he doesn’t discriminate
in terms of talent and employs from among the town’s various
immigrant populations, as well as Indigenous and African-American
workers. Unlike some other gangster crews, O’Bannion sees positive
community relations as a necessity for good business.
While bootlegging is the largest and most profitable element of
O’Bannion’s business, his empire stretches to loansharking, gambling,
prostitution, protection rackets, good old-fashioned robbery (if the
rewards warrant it), and so on. While O’Bannion oversees everything
(i.e., he expects money to flow to him), he has a cadre of lieutenants
who look after the day-to-day operations, each carving their own
niche and dreaming dreams of one day being the “big boss.”
Look to the Future
O’Bannion wants to put Joe Potrello (The Italian Club, 912) out of the
picture permanently, but is biding his time for the right conditions and
moment. Arkham is too small a town for an outright hit, but O’Bannion
feels sure that, if he is patient enough, his chance will come.
Notable Folk
M
Danny O’Bannion, 33, is (publicly) the owner-manager of Lucky
Clover Cartage, but he is also the overall boss of Arkham’s
organized crime. He originates from Boston, where he maintains
good relations with those who fronted him the money to set
up in Arkham.

431 UNCONSIDERED TRIFLES
240A W Church Street
Tucked away in a side alley, one might easily be unaware of this store’s
existence; indeed, many walk right past the alleyway each day without
knowledge of the treasures to be found within. An antique shop,
Unconsidered Trifles is a small concern but nevertheless is well regarded
in the local trade of historical items. From European furniture to early
colonial objects and memorabilia, as well as old books, oil paintings,
jewelry, and more, the shop is a dusty collection of valuables that would
interest the most serious of collectors. Open 10:00 am to 6:00 pm, closed
for two hours for lunch, Monday to Friday; occasionally open Saturday.
The owner’s office lies on the floor above the shop, and to the
rear of the premises, beyond the storefront, is a storeroom next to
a loading yard. In the storeroom is a door that leads down into a
copious basement filled with packing cases and a rackety old boiler
and furnace.
A Hidden Trade

deals in more questionable transactions, including the buying and selling

of goods of dubious origin. Such items, never seen in the front store,
are part of a healthy backroom trade with collectors around the world.

GET A HAT GET AHEAD
During the early 20th century, Americans were very
conscientious about wearing hats. It was right and
proper for both men and women to wear suitable head
attire when out and about, and one was simply “naked”
without a hat.
For ladies there was a wide range of choices and styles,
be it a “rolling brim” sailor’s hat, a drape hat, a feather
turban, pompon hat, or the very popular “bell-shaped”
cloche hat. The choices for men were perhaps a little less
varied, but a hat nonetheless enabled a gentleman to
express their personality (to a small degree) with their
hat choice.
It is interesting to note that there were distinct seasons
for hats: summer and winter. During winter, heavier, felt
hats were worn, while in summer, straw hats helped to
alleviate the heat. For men, straw boaters were the norm,
and most towns and cities had a particular day—”Straw
Hat Day”—when every man was expected to change into
the summer season’s headwear (mid-July in Arkham).
Likewise, “Felt Hat Day” (late September in Arkham)
announced the return to felt hats. Like in some other
places (like New York City), Arkham’s younger men seized
on the opportunity to grab the straw hat from another
man’s head and destroy it—if they were still wearing it
after Felt Hat Day. Such youthful misbehavior could, at
times, turn into a near riot, with mobs racing through
the streets and destroying straw boaters as they went—
injuries and arrests were likely.

Opal Rossini, 26, is a counter assistant and knows all the

505 EAST CHURCH, THE
444 E Main Street
This 1842 brick structure, owned by Miskatonic University, serves
as the University Chapel. Nondenominational services are held on
Sundays for the student and academic body. Many locals use the spire
to mark the boundary of River-Town and the Merchant District.
Thus, the spire is a useful navigation aid for those new to Arkham.
Notable Folk
M
Cecil Leach, 34, is the newly appointed young preacher.
506 ELEANOR PEABODY CHARITY HOME
173 N Powder Mill Street
A charity home for the destitute elderly. Residents receive three
meals a day and their general welfare needs are met. The home can
cater for around 30 residents, with a staff of 14 caregivers, cooks, and
cleaners. They serve meals in a communal dining room, and there
is a day room where activities are held. The home and its work are
funded by the late Eleanor Peabody’s estate.
Notable Folk
M
Harriet Nickels, 44, is the home’s manager; an ex-nurse who
runs the place with military-like precision.
M
Biddy Landers, 36, the sympathetic head cook.
Strangeness
The building was once the home of Geoffrey Sallow, an inventor
who rose briefly to fame in the early 1800s, although whose name
is now all but forgotten. When the Peabody estate took over the
property, they cleared the house, and, during this time, at least two
secret rooms were discovered that were then converted into open
spaces for the rest home. Some believe that Sallow had other secret
rooms or passageways in his home, although efforts to uncover more
hidden spaces have proved fruitless (so far). It is also rumored that
before his death, Sallow was working on some very strange projects,
but evidence of these have also never been found.
507 BARBERSHOP
403 E Church Street
Marked by the red and blue barber’s pole outside, here is where
many of Arkham’s gentlemen come to get their hair cut and enjoy
a wet shave while discussing the news of the day. Something of
a male retreat from the chaos of modern life, the interior smells
of cherry-flavored pipe tobacco. The furnishings are plush, with
leather-backed chairs, potted plants, marble counters, and a
congenial atmosphere. Open 8:00 am to 6:00 pm, Monday to
Saturday, closed Tuesday mornings.
Notable Folk

Willie Levard, 56, is the affable proprietor and head barber.
M

M
Atoy Wooten, 14, helps to keep the place clean with his broom
and wants to become a barber one day.

History
Schmidt emigrated to Arkham shortly after the end of the Great
War. He is a skilled craftsman, trained in stained-glass design and
construction. While he mostly works to the designs of his clients, he
enjoys creating magnificent stained-glass pieces of his own design.
Strangeness
Schmidt keeps a lookout for house sales and demolition work,
particularly if they concern grand old New England homes or
religious buildings. Occasionally, such places have stained glass
pieces that he can purchase and restore. In his time, he has
seen a handful of rather unusual “windows” crafted with bizarre
arrangements of colored glass or else presenting weird “art.” On
one occasion, when he ventured to look through such a piece,
he fancied he saw a strange landscape beyond, which sent an icy
shiver down his spine and caused him to suffer awful nightmares
for some days after.

chapter 4
Strangeness
In the 40-odd-years he’s ridden the byways of the town, Hiram has
witnessed many strange things and found even stranger things in
certain people’s trash—which he may “remember” for a small fee.
He also knows some details about the local bootlegging operation,
and his regular inspection of folks’ garbage tells him who Danny
O’Bannion’s (Lucky Clover Cartage Co., 412) best customers are.
517 DUNHAM’S BRICKYARD
700 E River Street
Closed since 1912, the brickyard was once second only to the
Miskatonic University as Arkham’s largest employer. Over the last
ten or so years, the yard has become a derelict place with its buildings
boarded up and decaying. It is now home to a youthful gang of
criminals called the Finns who use the most intact shack in the
yard as their headquarters.
Those wandering around the site, especially at night, are likely to
accosted by at least one gang member, who will first attempt to scare
them off, or else—and if they look moderately wealthy—try to mug
them. Those who show up looking for trouble will easily find it here.
Historical
The Finns are at the low-end of Arkham’s criminal fraternity, having
come together just a handful of years ago: a street gang that has yet
to evolve into anything more organized. They follow O’Bannion’s
operations with great interest and look up to him in an idealized
manner. Occasionally, someone in O’Bannion’s crew uses members
of the Finns to carry out a job (usually theft or robbery), and this
is a great way for up-and-coming members to get the attention of,
and potentially be recruited by, the “grown-ups” league.
Gang members indulge in petty thievery and occasional burglary,
but there’s no fence in Arkham who’ll trust these kids (yet). Thus,
they mostly loiter on corners and in vacant lots to talk and posture.
156

guide to arkham
Finns’ Rivalry
The Finns consider the area around the brickyard as their turf.
They tend to keep to River-Town and the northern parts of the
French Hill neighborhood as these are where they feel the safest,
due to their own-going rivalry with the Rocks, a gang of Italian
youths that congregates around the Southside Gym (717) on
South Sentinel Street. Members of both gangs hang out in Art’s
Billiards (220), which they consider neutral ground, although
that hasn’t stopped the occasional fight breaking out around the
billiards tables.

Similarly, College Street contains, besides some campus buildings, Bascom Jones

to the first settlement of Arkham.
601 MISKATONIC VALLEY VETERANS’ HOME
224 Boundary Street
A place of rest for those injured in war, be they veterans of the
Spanish-American War or the Great War. Whether physically
or mentally injured (or both), the home caters to those with
particularly grievous scars, such as triple and quadruple
amputations, devastating shrapnel and facial wounds, and those
whose bodies were incapacitated by poison gas. Many also suffer
mental trauma (“shellshock”) and have retreated here from the
world. Most are unlikely to ever return to their former lives.
Passersby may glimpse the residents, drifting ghost-like across
the windows.
The home, supported by community and church funds, is run
by Dr. Frederick Henks, himself a veteran of the war and who
possesses his own, albeit less severe, scars from the experience.
Henks is assisted by a team of six nurses, five orderlies, and a
cook. From time to time, medical students from the university
provide relief and assistance.
Notable Folk
M
Dr. Frederick Henks, 36, manages the home and tends to the
residents’ care.

618 GEORGE LOCKSLEY HALL
Miskatonic Campus
This red-brick Georgian building has the honor of being the oldest
building on campus, dating back to 1779. Despite its age, the
woodwork and furniture are in remarkably good shape. The building
contains lecture halls, classrooms, and minor offices. Students in the
College of LL&A take some of their classes in this building. Many
student clubs and campus organizations have offices and meeting
rooms here, too.
619 DOROTHY UPMAN HALL
Miskatonic Campus
In 1875, wealthy Arkhamite Dorothy Grace Upman offered the
university a sizeable endowment on the condition that women be
freely admitted to all courses of study at Miskatonic. The trustees
agreed, and part of the Upman Endowment went toward building a
women’s dormitory on campus. Since 1879, all female scholars have
been required to live here until age 30, unless they live with their
families or husbands. Given the amorous inclinations of the male
student body and the puritanical sensibilities of Arkham, Upman
Hall is arguably the most secure building on campus. Gentleman
callers are admitted only into the entrance lobby and not at all after
dark. The Upman Hall monitors are notorious for their draconian
enforcement of campus curfew.
Accommodation is split between one- and two-bedrooms, with
shared bathroom facilities on each floor. The rooms, communal
areas, and hallways are neat and clean, although due to cost
savings when under construction, the fixtures and fittings are not
the best and prone to wear and tear. There is a general curfew
of 10:00 pm.
Notable Folk
M
Wendy Allcart, 34, is dormitory supervisor and, due to her being
unmarried, lives on site.
620 EAST DORMITORY
Miskatonic Campus
Built in 1863 in a Gothic style, this imposing building is notable
for its circular stained-glass window above its entrance, as well as
the octopus plaque carved above the front door, known as “Oscar”
by the students within.
The East Dormitory is a male, lowerclassman’s dormitory.
All male freshmen attending Miskatonic are required to live
here unless they live with their family or in a relative’s home in
Arkham. The dormitory also hosts a few unfortunate sophomores
who can’t find lodgings anywhere else. Dismal plumbing, faulty
heating, a leaky roof, and the general bustle and commotion on
every floor have earned the building the nickname “Hell East.”
The dining hall, while a popular gathering place, serves the worst
meals on campus.
All the accommodation is two-bedroom, with shared
bathroom facilities on each floor. There is a general curfew
of 10:00 pm.

President Addleson retires in 1925 and is replaced by 48-year-old
Dr. Harvey Wainscott. Formerly a dean at Dartmouth, Wainscott
presides over a reorganization of the university in a modernizing
effort. In 1928, Wainscott stirs up Arkham by running for mayor
against longtime incumbent Joseph Peabody (Town Hall, 217).

708 UNIVERSITY SPA
311 S Garrison Street
The Spa is a student-oriented lunchroom offering reasonably priced
decent food. Thus, it’s usually full of students, leaving others with
no option but to wait their turn for a table or order for takeout. The
breakfast pancakes are the first choice for most, while the baked pork
chops and the meatloaf provide a hearty lunch for starving students.
Open 6:00 am to 3:30 pm, Monday to Saturday.
Notable Folk
M
Jadwiga Piotrowski, 47, is the owner and loves fussing over the
students: she is somewhat motherly and protective of her favorite
customers, often knowing more about them than their families.
709 MISKATONIC UNIVERSITY GARAGE
334 S Parsonage Street
A storage and repair facility for MU’s vehicles, although drivers can
store private cars here for a fee of $1 per week, subject to available
space. MU employs the mechanics here, so, in terms of priority, they
tend to service MU’s cars ahead of others. Open 7:30 am to 6:00
pm, closed for an hour at lunch, Monday to Saturday.

710 LEWISTON HOUSE HOTEL
181 E College Street
A small hotel renting out modest, clean rooms for $1.75 per night.
Cheaper block-booking rates are available by the week or month.
The hotel carefully scrutinizes all renters in an effort to avoid any
(new) scandal; young men who keep irregular hours will be evicted.
There’s one permanent resident, Mrs. Tabitha York, who only leaves
her room to eat.
Notable Folk
M
Marsha Lewiston, 53, is the owner and previously ran the hotel
with her husband, Matthew, before he passed six years ago. She,
like her husband, is particularly devout and tends to worry far
too much about “Godless youth” and the “wayward behavior of
those so-called Flappers.”
M
Tabitha York, 68, keeps to her room, only emerging to eat when
Mrs. Lewiston knocks on her door. Everyone assumes “Mrs.”
York was once married but, in truth, men were never her thing.
Besides that revelation, she has another secret—of once being
the high priestess of a cult worshipping Shub-Niggurath.

A three-story, brick-built theater, originally constructed in 1879 as
a vaudeville hall. The theater previously hosted touring companies
as well as local dramatic and singing groups. Ownership installed
a silver screen for motion pictures in 1916, changing it to a movie
theater, although its low attendance numbers suggest it has a lot of
work to do to achieve the size of audiences enjoyed by the Manley
Theater (106) and Amherst Theater (225).
The building’s layout comprises a lobby containing two ticket
booths, with double doors in the rear to the house seats. Stairs on
either side of the lobby lead to the upper floor’s balcony and box
seating, as well as the projection room. At the back of the building
(behind the movie screen) are old dressing rooms, an office, and
the stage mechanics. The rear of the second floor contains storage,
rehearsal rooms, and the theater’s old props room. The third floor
has access to the wing perch (a platform to the catwalks above the

and bequests from Arkham natives.

the Pickering House (301) on Federal Street.

Gaspard’s Great Work
Jason Gaspard is working on a new text, drawing on his research at
the Orne Library and inspiration from his dreams. It is a work in
progress, comprising around 100 loose, typewritten pages of varying
quality in terms of its contents. How useful or what it contains
of value is left to the Keeper’s determination. One possibility is
that Gaspard’s dream inspiration is actually stemming from an

anyone’s guess.

What’s Going On?
Giuseppe “Joe”
The café is the base of operations for what’s left of Joe Potrello’s criminal
enterprise. He drinks coffee and wine while plotting impossible revenges Potrello
against Danny O’Bannion and his gang (Lucky Clover Cartage Co., Diminished Gangster, age 34
412). From here, he runs numbers and race-betting operations and
deals in stolen items (though not items stolen from Italians), which STR 75 APP 65
select patrons may purchase here. Rumor has it that Potrello must now CON 60 POW 75
funnel a significant share of his profits to O’Bannion.
SIZ 70 EDU 45
Notable Folk DEX 60 SAN 61
M
Virgilio “Big Red” Scavo, 49, is the manager; a portly fellow INT 75
with a stare that could kill.
M
Isabetta Scavo, 46, is Virgilio’s wife who does all the cooking
while her husband chats and serves coffee. HP 13
M
Giuseppe “Joe” Potrello, 42, the former criminal “boss” of Arkham. DB +1D4
M
Lou Benito, 29, Potrello’s henchman and bodyguard. Build 1
Move 7
MP 15
Potrello is a sorry sight these days. His power evaporated, his
influence and bootlegging operation are gone, and he has one
loyal henchman left. Not even the Italian youth gang, the Rocks
(Southside Gym, 717), respects him anymore. He knows the
O’Bannion mob has him marked for death. He also knows that
police are on O’Bannion’s payroll and so fears that they might set
him up (not true, Arkham’s police are not yet that corrupt).
Potrello came to the US in 1900 at the age of 12, sent here by his
widower father to live with relatives in Arkham. He grew up in Arkham’s
poorest Italian community, working in mills here and in nearby Bolton.
By age 18, he led a handful of toughs specializing in muggings and
shopkeeper extortion. Dismissed from the Army after a few weeks (he
joined just before the signing of the armistice), Potrello established an
ingenious illegal numbers game modeled on rackets popular in New
York City. The game turned a tidy profit and, when Prohibition arrived,
Potrello had the capital and contacts to locally distribute profitable booze
from overseas. Despite “owning” the town, he did not see O’Bannion
coming and in the blink of an eye, he lost Arkham.
M
Description: dressed in common working-class clothes, he
possesses a rather splendid mustache and is thin of frame.
M
Traits: a modest man, cool and shrewd, he plays the long game
and could, if fortune favors him, one day end up elected to
the Town Council. To those who have wronged him, he is a
stern opponent and merciless.

915 MORNINGSIDE FUNERAL PARLOR
503 S Sentinel Street
This funeral parlor is in an archaic-looking, peak-roofed, two-story
building. The front of the building sports a rudimentary garden
consisting of weeping willow and various bushes, along with a
somewhat disconcerting display of headstones.
Morningside provides funeral services, including cremation, at a
somewhat lower costs that most other funeral homes in Arkham.
Beyond the first-floor reception area is a viewing chapel with
seating, a lounge-cum-meeting room, and office that contains a
door leading to two adjoining embalming rooms. The second floor
contains a display room of different styles of coffins, a storage
room containing funerary chemicals and equipment, and the
private bedrooms and lounge of the owner, Casey Grescht, and
his employee, Brady Whitcombe.
Notable Folk
M
Casey Grescht, 44, is the sweaty funeral director and a mortician.
He is close friends with William Danvers Johnson (page 53),
vice-president of the Arkham First Bank (214).
M
Brady Whitcombe, 22, is underpaid and overworked and
carries items to and fro at Grescht’s bidding. He is an ugly and
distasteful chap, who served two years in jail for vandalism and
petty larceny while a teenager.
Look to the Future
By 1928, Grescht is an associate of the Arkham Coven (page 51),
and he is next in line to enter the inner circle of 13 members. One
possible and grisly outcome for Grescht is detailed in the scenario
“Dark Rivals” (originally published by Chaosium in Dead Reckonings).
916 PINTER’S VETERINARY PRACTICE
184 E Saltonstall Street
A veterinary practice operating out of the home of “Doc” Pinter.
Many in Arkham consider Pinter the best vet in town, with an
exceptional knowledge of both pet and farm livestock conditions.
He is reasonably priced, occasionally providing his services for free
to those less fortunate. The practice’s normal hours are 9:00 am to
5:00 pm, Monday to Friday, although Pinter does tend to work half
days on Saturdays, traveling out to farms to attend to livestock. In
emergencies, he is happy to open up or visit a home if necessary.
The first floor of the house contains an examination room,
treatment room, and a study. Customers can wait in the hallway
where a few chairs are available. Pinter’s kitchen is at the rear, and
his bedroom and other private rooms are on the second floor.

Strangeness
The ancient archway carved in the wall is a Gate to other worlds
and dimensions. Randolph Carter used this portal to travel beyond,
as noted in the Lovecraft story “Through the Gates of the Silver
Key” written with E. Hoffmann Price.
Should the investigators possess the silver key (or another like
it), they may pass through the Gate to a destination of their choice,
including Earth’s Dreamlands and others. Those without a silver
key may attempt to use the Gate with a successful Cthulhu Mythos
roll, although only an Extreme success enables them to dictate their

guide to arkham
OS118 ARKHAM AIRFIELD
This flying field is owned by ex-ace Florence Harrington. It consists
of a short, dirt runway, a hangar with doors at either end, two planes,
a small office beside the hangar, and a windsock. The planes are,
respectively, a two-seat ex-military Curtiss JN “Jenny” and an old
Rex Smith Biplane capable of carrying two passengers plus the pilot.
The planes are available for hire, with Harrington piloting ($2 per
mile), or renting to a licensed pilot or someone able to demonstrate
their ability (Pilot Aircraft skill of at least 30%)—rental requires a
$50 deposit and Harrington’s approval of the applicant’s character;
hourly rental charges are $2 and $3, respectively, for the two-seater
and the three-seater, and renters pay for gasoline and any damage.
She will negotiate day rates. Harrington is happy to store planes in
her hangar for $1 a week, plus maintenance charges if applicable.
Instruction
Harrington is a qualified flight instructor who can teach Pilot Aircraft
to people of whom she approves, but they must have a DEX of at least
65. The price for a three-hour lesson, once per week is $7.50, with the
course lasting six months. At the end of that time the student gains
+3D10+10 percentiles in Pilot Aircraft. Advanced lessons at $65 per
month raise the student’s ability by +5 percentiles every six months,
to a maximum of 60%. Notably, Wingate Peaslee (School of Natural
Sciences, 612-A) is currently taking flying lessons with Harrington.
In the future, he aims to purchase his own plane.
Notable Folk
M
Florence Harrington, 28,
is the airfield’s owner and a
notable pilot. A Boston native,
Harrington has toured as a
barnstormer and worked as a
crop duster and mail carrier.
After a near-fatal crash, she
decided to settle down, and
used her money to open the
Arkham Airfield.

Harrington’s mechanic; short,
plump, and friendly. Bessie is
something of an engineering
whizz. Key skills: Airplane
Repair 85%, Electrical Repair
75%, Mechanical Repair 90%.
Useful
Carefully greased and hidden away in the hangar is a .30
machine gun (as used in the Great War) with 5,000 rounds of
ammunition, acquired by Harrington in a card game. She could
fit the weapon to either of her two planes.

farm, destroying his barn and three-quarters of his cattle. 1931 (January 24): Atwood and Lake fall victim to the horrors
in Antarctica.
1928 (September 13): The Dunwich Horror wipes out the Elmer
Frye family at 3:00 am. 1931 (March): A gale destroys the roof of Arkham’s now-deserted
Witch House.
1928 (September 13): After a short visit with his “friend” Akeley,
Wilmarth escapes the Vermont farmhouse in terror of what he 1933: Daniel Upton shoots Edward Pickman Derby dead.
has learned.
1935: Miskatonic’s expedition to the Western Australia desert begins.
1928 (September 14): Armitage, Rice, and Morgan set out for
Dunwich by motorcar. They learn of the destruction of the Frye farm

biographies
Biographies
Mike Mason Keith Herber
Mike Mason is an award-winning game writer and the creative Keith “Doc” Herber (1949–2009) was an author, editor, and
director at Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. musician, heralding from Detroit, Michigan. Keith was the
Mike is the co-writer of the current edition of the Call of Cthulhu Call of Cthulhu line editor at Chaosium in the late 80s to early
roleplaying game (7th edition), Pulp Cthulhu, and the lead writer/ 90s and worked on the fifth edition of the game and numerous
designer of the Call of Cthulhu Starter Set, Malleus Monstrorum (2nd supplements. Notable works include The Fungi from Yuggoth (1984),
edition), and the revised Masks of Nyarlathotep. Traces of Mike’s Trail of Tsathoggua (1984), Spawn of Azathoth (1986), and Keeper’s
tentacles can be found in every book in the line. Compendium (1993). Perhaps his most-loved work was the creation
Around the millennium, Mike published The Whisperer, a of the “Lovecraft Country” line of setting books for Call of Cthulhu,
fanzine devoted to Call of Cthulhu, and ran the Kult of Keepers, beginning with Arkham Unveiled (1990). He also helped launch
a group of Call of Cthulhu scenario writers organizing convention Chaosium’s well-loved “Cycle” fiction line. His scenario, “Edge of
games. Mike previously worked for Games Workshop as the Line Darkness” remains one of the prime introductory scenarios for the
Manager and co-writer of the ENNIE Award winning Warhammer game and is currently available in the Call of Cthulhu Starter Set.
40,000 RPG: Dark Heresy, as well as working on Warhammer Fantasy Keith also worked on books for White Wolf’s Vampire: The
Roleplay. Mike lives in the Midlands of England, betwixt the rolling Masquerade line, including Prince of the City (1995) and Dark Prince
Derbyshire Peaks and the Satanic Mills of Nottinghamshire, with (1994), as well as fiction novels and the Tremere Clanbook (1994).
a grumpy cat called Stripey. He later returned to Call of Cthulhu in the late 2000s, starting up
Miskatonic River Press to publish new Call of Cthulhu scenarios
under license, releasing New Tales of the Miskatonic Valley (2008).
“Doc” Herber was also an enthusiastic bass guitarist, playing
with rock and blues bands across the United States, such as The
Fabulous Thunderbirds and Detroit’s Progressive Blues Band.
Keith passed in Lakeland, Florida, 2009, aged 60. His energy
and insights are missed.

On the streets of Arkham, the threat of the Cthulhu Mythos is ever-present.
A quiet town in New England—home to the prestigious Miskatonic University—
Arkham’s underbelly hides criminals, speakeasies, and a witch-cursed history.
Arkham is the definitive guide to the signature setting of Call of Cthulhu.
M
A sandbox campaign setting for Call of Cthulhu.
M
The history of Arkham and the Miskatonic University.
M
Details of 9 neighborhoods, with over 290 locations described.
M
New rules and skills for Arkham investigators.
M
More than 80 fully-detailed NPCs.
M
Gossip and rumors to use as scenario seeds for original stories.
M
Street and neighborhood maps, as well as floorplans of
key locations.
M

marked with information for the Keeper.

For Mature Readers: contains mature themes and is intended
for mature players.
This supplement is part of the Arkham Unveiled line and is
designed for use with both the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game
and the Pulp Cthulhu supplement, both available separately.
What is Call of Cthulhu?
Call of Cthulhu is Chaosium’s roleplaying game of mystery and
horror set within the world of the Cthulhu Mythos. Players take on
the role of investigators of the strange, arcane, and unknown: regular
people making a stand despite the cost to body and soul. Against
weird cults, bizarre magic, and otherworldly monsters, only they can
save humanity and the world from the terrors from beyond.
